The Department of State Services has asked the Federal High Court in Abuja to foreclose the defence of the presidential candidate of the African Action Congress, Omoyele Sowore, over alleged delays in his ongoing cyberbullying trial. The DSS, through its counsel, Akinlolu Kehinde (SAN), on Tuesday urged Justice Mohammed Umar to grant an application seeking to close the defendant’s case, alleging that he had exceeded the number of adjournments permitted under the law. Kehinde told the court that the application, filed on November 23, had been served on Sowore’s legal team, adding that the defendant had sought or procured adjournments on at least 14 occasions since the commencement of the trial. He argued that the number was far beyond the five adjournments permitted under Section 396(4) of the Administration of Criminal Justice Act, 2015. “Before we finally draw the curtain on the proceedings, I want to bring to your lordship’s notice the application we filed and served on the defendant. “The application is that there must be an end to all these. The defendant has since exceeded the number of adjournments as required by law,” he said. In the motion on notice, the DSS sought an order closing the defence’s case and directing the parties to file and exchange their final written addresses within a period to be determined by the court, ahead of a date for their adoption. Giving nine grounds in support of the application, Kehinde said Sowore was re-arraigned on a two-count charge on January 19, 2026, to which he pleaded not guilty, after which the trial commenced. He said the prosecution called its witness and closed its case in March 2026, while the court dismissed Sowore’s no-case submission on May 8, 2026, and directed him to enter his defence. According to the prosecution, Sowore subsequently sought or procured adjournments on at least 14 occasions, eight of which occurred after he was called upon to open his defence. Kehinde said the trial had made little progress since Sowore opened his defence on July 6, 2026, with only two defence witnesses having testified. “Since the defendant/respondent opened his defence on 6th July 2026, the trial has not progressed beyond the evidence of two defence witnesses,” he said. He said the court had, on several occasions, cautioned the defendant against delaying the trial. Kehinde argued that the constitutional right to a fair hearing did not confer an unlimited right to adjournments, stressing that a defendant who had been given sufficient opportunity to present his case could not complain of a breach of that right. “Section 36(4) of the Constitution guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time, and the Administration of Criminal Justice Act, 2015 requires that criminal trials proceed from day to day or, where that is impracticable, within the strict limits on adjournments prescribed by Section 396 of the ACJA.” He urged the court to grant the application in the interest of justice. However, Sowore’s counsel, Reuben Adakole, opposed the timing of the application, arguing that the court should first determine pending applications relating to the subpoena issued against the Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission, Prof. Joash Amupitan (SAN). Adakole acknowledged receiving the DSS application but maintained that the court needed to deliver its ruling on Amupitan’s application to set aside the subpoena, as well as the defence’s preliminary objection and ex-parte motion, before considering the prosecution’s request. “Inasmuch as the application tends to foreclose us, there is our application which the court ought to pronounce on first. Until after the ruling, we can look at it. The application is unripe, my lord,” he said. 2027 election: Delta killings heighten fears of poll violence ‘Tinubu’s phone call saved Buhari from 2015 disqualification’ ‘Exorcising’ INEC’s ghost voters Meanwhile, Alex Iziyon (SAN), who represented Amupitan, informed the court that the matter had previously been adjourned because the defence had yet to file its counter-affidavit. He, however, confirmed that the defence had subsequently filed the process and that he had responded, urging the parties to adopt their respective processes. Adakole confirmed that the processes had been exchanged but clarified that the subpoena issued to the INEC chairman was strictly a subpoena duces tecum, requiring him to produce documents rather than appear as a witness to give oral evidence. “It is just strictly to come and tender the documents, and that was why we filed a motion to amend the application. “We ask that we be allowed to move our motion ex parte, so that it will lay to rest all these issues. “So the intent was just for the INEC chairman to tender the documents and not to testify,” he said. Iziyon disagreed, accusing the defence of attempting to circumvent the court’s earlier directive. “The defendant cannot take this court for a ride. I submit with all sense of responsibility,” he said. He reminded the court that it had directed the defence to file a formal application on notice to enable the opposing parties to respond. In response, Justice Umar told Adakole that the defence was required to comply with the court’s directive since the parties had already joined issues on the matter. “Before the last adjourned date, I told you that since you have issued that subpoena and they have been joined, anything you want to do now will be by motion on notice; serve them, and they will respond,” the judge said. The court subsequently heard the applications, with Iziyon adopting three processes filed on behalf of Amupitan and urging the court to set aside the subpoena. He relied on an earlier ruling by Justice Umar on the court’s power to set aside a subpoena and cited a previous case in which a subpoena was set aside because the person sought to be summoned had no connection with the subject matter of the proceedings. Adakole, in his response, adopted the defence processes and urged the court to dismiss Amupitan’s application. He also moved an ex parte application filed on November 11, seeking four reliefs, arguing that the documents requested were public records in the custody of a public officer and were necessary for Sowore’s defence. He maintained that their relevance could only be determined by the court after they had been produced. “It is not for the applicant to say so. That will be preemptive,” he said. After listening to the parties, Justice Umar adjourned the case until December 7 for ruling on Amupitan’s application to set aside the subpoena. The judge also fixed the date for the hearing of the DSS application seeking to foreclose Sowore’s defence and other pending applications.
